question: Can a random-feature model learn a useful activation function from data while retaining the computational and statistical advantages of fixed random features?

key_findings.claim: RFLAF separates directional randomness from activation learning by optimizing only shared basis coefficients and output weights.
key_findings.evidence: The model draws M Gaussian directions once, expands a univariate activation in N fixed radial-basis, spline, or polynomial functions, and learns N activation coefficients plus M output coefficients. This is a low-parameter bilinear adaptation of a random-feature map rather than first-layer feature learning.

key_findings.claim: A single non-centered Gaussian RBF activation has an analytic rotation-invariant kernel but does not by itself solve the expressivity bottleneck.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems 3.1-3.2 derive the kernel and its tensor feature expansion; Corollary 3.3 characterizes its represented functions. The authors explicitly note fast-decaying coefficients and a narrow class, motivating a learnable mixture of RBFs.

key_findings.claim: The approximation and generalization guarantees are existence results under a compactly supported Lipschitz target activation and norm-constrained factors.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.1 approximates the unknown activation on a fixed compact interval with a fine Gaussian grid; Theorem 4.2 combines this error with finite random-feature sampling. Theorem 5.1 bounds excess risk for Lipschitz loss over a constrained bilinear class, yielding M on the order of the square root of sample size after its prescribed scaling.

key_findings.claim: Across seven tabular and vision benchmarks, small learned RBF or spline dictionaries usually improve on fixed-activation random features at modest added cost.
key_findings.evidence: With M=1,000 or 3,000 and N=16, Table 1 reports RBF/spline RFLAF as best or near-best on MNIST, CIFAR-10, Adult, Protein, CT, Workloads, and MillionSongs. RBF inference is roughly 1.0-2.4 times the ReLU RF reference, while spline inference is 1.4-7.3 times; experiments average ten seeds.

key_findings.claim: The empirical benefit is not yet isolated from hyperparameter budget, optimization, and basis-selection effects.
key_findings.evidence: The learned models receive a grid-size sweep and bespoke regularizers, whereas fixed activations are a short hand-selected list; there is no equal-search-budget neural-kernel or activation-search comparison. Polynomial divergence is counted as failure, and test-error minima are used to report convergence epochs in an overfitting study.

method.core_idea: Parameterize one shared scalar activation as a learned linear combination of fixed universal basis functions, apply it to many frozen random projections, and jointly learn its coefficients with the output weights.
method.mechanism: For Gaussian directions w_m, RFLAF predicts the average of v_m times the basis expansion sum_i a_i B_i(w_m^T x). A Gaussian grid gives an approximation argument for compactly supported activations; concentration controls finite M, and Rademacher complexity controls empirical-risk generalization. Training uses MSE or cross-entropy plus a factor-balancing penalty and optional L1 sparsity on activation coefficients.
assumptions: The target belongs to a random-feature integral class with a compactly supported Lipschitz activation and Lipschitz coefficient function.
Gaussian random directions and a prespecified basis interval, centers, widths, and grid resolution are appropriate for the data.
The bilinear nonconvex optimizer finds a useful solution inside or near the norm-constrained class used by the theory.
Mean performance over ten random seeds captures relevant variability despite dataset and hyperparameter selection effects.

techniques.role: Adds only N global coefficients to adapt the nonlinear feature map.
Provides a universal univariate approximation family with analytically tractable induced kernels.
Bounds error from replacing the Gaussian feature integral by M sampled directions.
Controls scale non-identifiability between activation and output coefficient vectors.
Connects constrained RFLAF empirical risk to population risk.

evaluations.setting: Seven classification/regression datasets with fixed random projections, M=1,000 or 3,000, and N=16 learned basis functions.
evaluations.metric: Cross-entropy or squared test loss, relative train/test time, mean and standard deviation across ten seeds.
evaluations.result: RBF and B-spline RFLAF variants are consistently competitive with or better than fixed ReLU, cosine, tanh, and sigmoid RF baselines; gains are especially large on Workloads and CT.
evaluations.baseline: Same-width fixed-activation random-feature MLPs and polynomial-basis RFLAF.

evaluations.setting: Grid-size ablation with N in 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128, plus synthetic recovery of a piecewise sinusoidal activation at N=400.
evaluations.metric: Test error, normalized time, epoch of minimum test loss, and plotted activation recovery.
evaluations.result: Error generally falls as N grows while runtime grows linearly; the synthetic learned activation visually tracks the ground truth.
evaluations.baseline: Smaller RBF dictionaries and the known synthetic activation.

evaluations.setting: Unfrozen first-layer two-layer networks, where RFLAF becomes LAN, on the same datasets.
evaluations.metric: Test loss and normalized inference time.
evaluations.result: RBF/spline LAN is generally best or near-best and avoids KAN's very poor results on CT and Workloads, though neither interpretability nor modern deep architectures are tested.

limitations: The strongest theory assumes a compactly supported Lipschitz target activation and prior knowledge sufficient to place an increasingly fine basis grid around it.
The approximation prescription can require N of the same order as M, whereas the practical claim that N=16 suffices is empirical and task-specific.
Joint learning is bilinear and nonconvex, but the existence/generalization results do not establish convergence of the implemented optimizer.
Experiments cover shallow random-feature or two-layer networks, modest vision/tabular benchmarks, and no ImageNet-scale or transformer-scale setting.
Baseline tuning budgets, validation protocol, parameter/compute accounting, and statistical significance tests are not fully reported.
The activation is shared across every random direction, which is efficient but may prevent heterogeneous feature specialization.
failure_modes: The useful activation lies outside the chosen compact interval or requires more basis resolution than the selected N.
Narrow RBFs make optimization ill-conditioned or produce almost inactive features for the sampled projections.
Scale swapping between a and v destabilizes training despite the balancing penalty.
Polynomial dictionaries explode at moderate degree, as observed on five datasets.
A fixed activation matched to the task wins once both families receive equal hyperparameter search and compute.
reusable_insights: Adapt a large frozen feature bank through a small shared nonlinear dictionary before paying to learn every feature direction.
Separate basis-approximation error, Monte Carlo feature error, and sample generalization error in theory and evaluation.
Report learning gains against an equal-search-budget fixed-feature oracle, not only a few conventional activations.
Use synthetic ground-truth recovery to audit whether learned parameterizations are identifiable, then test whether recovery predicts downstream performance.
Balance factor norms explicitly whenever a model is invariant to reciprocal rescaling of two parameter blocks.
open_questions: Can data-dependent basis centers and widths improve efficiency without breaking tractable generalization guarantees?
Does the learned activation transfer across datasets, random seeds, widths, or layers?
What optimization guarantees are possible for the bilinear RFLAF objective with balancing and sparsity penalties?
How does RFLAF compare with optimized fixed activations, multiple-kernel learning, and KAN/LAN variants at equal FLOPs and tuning budget?
Can direction-specific low-rank activation mixtures retain parameter efficiency while increasing specialization?

competitive_landscape.title: Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines
competitive_landscape.difference: Rahimi and Recht approximate a fixed shift-invariant kernel with sampled features. RFLAF instead learns a shared activation dictionary, thereby selecting a feature kernel from data while retaining frozen directions.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Activation Functions: A New Paradigm for Understanding Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This prior work learns activations from polynomial bases in ordinary neural networks. RFLAF supplies random-feature approximation/generalization analysis and finds polynomial instability, favoring localized RBFs or splines.

competitive_landscape.title: Searching for Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Activation search discovers a discrete computation graph through task-level search. RFLAF performs differentiable coefficient learning in a fixed universal basis and is much cheaper, but explores a narrower structured family.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: KAN places a separate learnable spline on each edge for high expressivity and interpretability. LAN/RFLAF shares one activation dictionary across units, trading edge-level flexibility for lower cost and easier scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal Activation Functions for the Random Features Regression Model
competitive_landscape.difference: This ICLR 2023 paper analytically characterizes task-optimal fixed activations for random-feature regression. RFLAF learns a basis mixture directly from finite data across broader tasks, avoiding a prespecified target distribution but adding nonconvex estimation and tuning.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first analytic kernel for a general non-centered Gaussian-RBF activation, approximation and generalization theory for learnable-activation random features, and a practical activation module that outperforms fixed RF models.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 3-5 provide kernel, approximation, and excess-risk theorems; Section 6 compares RBF/spline/polynomial dictionaries with fixed activations and extends the module to two-layer LANs.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Learnable and searched activations, spline networks, task-optimal random-feature activations, and KAN are established. The credible novelty is their specific shared basis-mixture random-feature formulation plus its RBF-kernel and statistical analysis. Empirical superiority is promising but not yet a scale or equal-tuning-budget result.

reviewer_notes: Read the 49-page cached manuscript, including all main theorems, experiment tables, appendices, and references. Competitors were checked against arXiv, OpenReview, and official NeurIPS primary pages on 2026-08-23. The review distinguishes existence/generalization statements from optimizer convergence and treats the claimed square-root feature scaling only under the paper's assumptions.
